lessons.title: Associate ordered keys with values
lessons.summary: Replace the find/first-print statements with std::cout << scores["Zed"] << " " << scores.size() << "\n";. What changes?
explanation: A std::map<Key,Value> keeps one value for each distinct key and visits keys in comparator order. Here strings use their usual lexicographic ordering, so Ada comes before Mina, regardless of insertion order.
find(key) returns an iterator or end() when absent. Comparing with end() before dereferencing avoids using a missing element. find does not add a key.
operator[] is different: scores["Zed"] inserts the missing key with a value-initialized int, which is 0. Use find or contains for observation; use [] when insertion is intended.
The structured binding const auto& [name, score] gives names to the existing pair’s key and value. It does not copy the whole map. The map key cannot be reassigned through this pair.

Expected output or behavior: 1 2
Ada:2
Mina:4. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Use hashed key lookup
lessons.summary: Replace the contains line with ++visits["lake"]; bool present = visits.contains("lake");. What prints?
explanation: An unordered_map associates keys with values using a hash function and key equality. Lookup is average constant time, but worst-case linear; that is not a promise about wall-clock speed.
Its iteration order is not sorted or insertion order. Rehashing may change that order and invalidate iterators. Do not use an observed order as the expected answer of a portable program.
contains(key) reports whether the key exists without changing the map. As with map, [] inserts a missing key and value-initializes the value; ++visits["lake"] therefore changes a new 0 to 1.

explanation: C++23 std::expected<T,E> contains either a successful T or an error E. It is useful when the caller should inspect a recoverable failure as part of the function’s return contract.

lessons.title: Handle exceptions at a boundary
lessons.summary: Pass -1 instead of 3 to checkedReward. Which output is correct?
explanation: throw signals a failure and transfers control toward a matching handler. Statements after the throwing operation inside that try block are skipped; a failed call does not supply its normal return value.

try encloses work that this boundary can handle. catch(const std::invalid_argument& error) handles that exception type without copying it. what() provides a descriptive string, not a machine-readable application protocol.

When stack unwinding occurs, destructors of fully constructed automatic objects in exited scopes run. Prefer RAII for cleanup. After this handler finishes normally, execution continues after the catch; an uncaught exception can terminate the program.

lessons.title: State exception guarantees honestly
lessons.summary: Instead, push directly into scores, then throw for a negative value, with no rollback. After adding -2, what does the catch leave?

addValidated builds a separate vector candidate. Copying, allocation or validation can fail before scores is changed. The final swap commits the prepared result; swapping these default-allocator vectors does not throw.

Replacing the candidate operations with direct edits to scores changes the guarantee. Catching the validation exception does not undo a previously successful push_back. noexcept also does not mean success: an escaping exception from a noexcept function terminates.

lessons.title: Evaluate constants and assert at compile time
lessons.summary: Change twice(3) to twice(4) but keep static_assert(size == 6). What happens?
explanation: A constexpr function can participate in constant evaluation when its inputs and operations permit it. Calling that function does not by itself force every call to happen at compile time.
constexpr int size = twice(3) requires a constant expression. By contrast, an ordinary int can hold a runtime result even when the called function is declared constexpr.

lessons.title: Separate declarations into headers
lessons.summary: Remove the guard lines from score.hpp but keep both includes. What happens in this translation unit?
explanation: A header is text included into a translation unit (one source file after preprocessing its includes). A declaration tells the compiler about a name and its type. A class definition such as struct Score may also live in a header when the language’s definition rules are respected.

Save this as score.hpp beside main.cpp:
```cpp
#ifndef SCORE_HPP
#define SCORE_HPP
struct Score { int value; };
#endif
```
The first inclusion defines SCORE_HPP. On the second inclusion, #ifndef is false, so the guarded definition is skipped. These preprocessor directives are not runtime if statements.

The source below intentionally includes the header twice. Compile main.cpp with the header available to the compiler. Use standard include guards rather than relying on a particular compiler’s #pragma once extension for this example.

lessons.title: Use diagnostics and sanitizers responsibly
lessons.summary: With this course’s -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror flags, add int unused = 7; inside main and never use it. What should you do with the build result?
explanation: Use -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic to request useful GCC diagnostics. They do not mean every possible warning is enabled. This course also uses -Werror, which treats emitted warnings as build errors rather than silently accepting them.

A local build with -g -fsanitize=address,undefined can instrument checks for supported memory and undefined-behavior errors. It only checks paths that actually execute; a clean run does not prove the whole program safe. Tool availability and platform support matter.

The worked array iteration stays in bounds. We do not execute invalid indexing or dangling-pointer examples. To demonstrate a rejected build safely, the changed case adds a genuinely unused variable; the configured warning policy rejects it before any run.

lessons.title: Test behavior with assertions
lessons.summary: Change the middle assertion to doubleSmall(2) == 5 and define NDEBUG before <cassert>. What can the final message prove?
explanation: An assertion states a condition that must hold at that point. These small tests cover zero, positive and negative inputs within a safe integer range; they are not exhaustive proof for every int.

With assertions enabled, a false assert prints a diagnostic and aborts. Keep tests small enough that a failure points toward a specific expectation. Production test frameworks can report many cases more conveniently.

Defining NDEBUG before including <cassert> disables assert checks. The expression is not evaluated then, so never put required side effects inside assert. A success message printed by a build with disabled assertions is not evidence that those conditions were checked.

lessons.title: Measure durations with chrono
lessons.summary: Change 1750 milliseconds to 2500 milliseconds. What whole-seconds count prints?
explanation: std::chrono::duration represents a count together with a tick period. milliseconds{1750} is not the bare integer 1750 seconds. count() returns the stored count in that duration’s own unit.
duration_cast<seconds> converts this integer millisecond duration to whole seconds. The fractional part is discarded toward zero, so 1750 milliseconds becomes 1 second, not a rounded 2.

For real elapsed timing, subtract two steady_clock::now() time points and convert the resulting duration. A monotonic clock is suited to elapsed time, but workload timings still vary; this deterministic example converts a supplied duration instead of promising a benchmark result.

lessons.title: Generate bounded random values
lessons.summary: Change die to {4,4} and replace the range check with roll == 4. What does the check print?
explanation: A random engine supplies pseudorandom state transitions. A distribution maps those engine results to values for a requested distribution. uniform_int_distribution<int>{1,6} includes both endpoints.

Seeding mt19937 with 42 gives the engine a repeatable initial state. Distribution algorithms can differ across standard-library implementations, so do not require the same displayed dice sequence on every toolchain.

This example checks that every generated value stays in the inclusive interval. Twenty rolls cannot establish that a generator is statistically fair, and mt19937 is not a cryptographic generator. Use application-appropriate randomness rather than a security claim.

lessons.title: Give a thread a joining lifetime
lessons.summary: Change the worker assignment to result = 12, keeping the scopes. May the final output still be the initial 0 because scheduling is slow?
explanation: A std::jthread starts work whose scheduling is independent of the following statements. Do not assume the worker has already completed just because its constructor returned.

When a joinable jthread is destroyed, it requests stop and joins. Joining waits for that thread to finish. A stop request is cooperative, not forced interruption; this small lambda simply returns normally.

The zero-argument lambda [&result] { ... } captures result by reference; the empty parameter list () is optional here. result is outside the worker’s scope, so it remains alive until after the worker is joined. The main thread reads it only after joining; it does not race with the worker’s write.

lessons.title: Protect shared state with a mutex
lessons.summary: Remove only the finalLock line, keeping every worker lock and both joins. Is the final read safe?
explanation: Concurrent conflicting access to a non-atomic object, without the required synchronization, can be a data race and undefined behavior. We do not run an unlocked competing-write example.

The lambda capture [&] borrows the surrounding locals it uses by reference; count and mutex remain alive beyond both joins. Every worker increment here holds the same mutex. lock_guard locks on construction and unlocks on destruction, including when its scope exits. Its lifetime covers the entire ++count operation, not only a separate read.

Both jthreads are destroyed and joined before the final read. Therefore no worker still writes count at that point. The final read’s extra lock is harmless but unnecessary here; removing the worker locks would be a different, unsafe change.

lessons.title: Update a simple counter atomically
lessons.summary: Change only the final fetch_add(3) to fetch_add(5). Which pair prints?
explanation: std::atomic<int> supports indivisible accesses to this one counter. fetch_add(1) is an atomic read-modify-write: competing updates do not lose an increment as a separate load followed by store could.
fetch_add(amount) adds amount but returns the previous value. After both workers finish 100 increments, fetch_add(3) returns 200 while the counter becomes 203.

This example keeps the default sequentially consistent ordering. It does not teach custom memory-order or lock-free design. Individual atomic variables do not automatically preserve a multi-variable invariant; mutex-protected groups of operations may still be needed.

lessons.title: Receive an asynchronous result
lessons.summary: Change the last async argument from false to true. Where is calculation failed handled?
explanation: std::async returns a future associated with the invoked function’s result. Explicit std::launch::async requests asynchronous execution rather than leaving the choice between deferred and asynchronous policy to the implementation.
future::get waits as necessary and retrieves the value. For an ordinary future it consumes the result; do not call get a second time as if it were a reusable cache.

If the asynchronous function throws, the exception is stored and rethrown when get retrieves the result. Catch it around get when this boundary can handle it. Asynchronous execution does not guarantee better performance or a particular completion time.

lessons.title: Build a bounded console game-state engine
lessons.summary: Change the second command from collect to quit, leaving the final collect. What state prints?
explanation: This tiny console model receives a command and returns the next Game value. apply takes state by value, so the caller must assign the returned state. Fixed test commands replace interactive input; this is not a graphics engine.

The initial state has two turns. A collect command increases score and consumes one turn; reaching zero stops play. quit stops without consuming a turn, and an unknown command leaves state unchanged. Once stopped, later commands do nothing.

For states reached from this initializer, at most two successful collects occur, so the score and turn arithmetic stays bounded. Test early quit, unknown commands and extra commands after stopping. A production app must also validate state loaded from untrusted storage; this function does not accept arbitrary states as valid.
